elements.title: Overdrive

data.name: Overdrive
data.pitch: A Training drill where targets spawn on the beat of your own songs. They come as a mix of types, such as shaped flick targets and player figures that strafe in time with the music, and each vanishes if you don't hit it in time. A mix of Beat Saber and Guitar Hero in a synthwave world, built as an aim trainer.
data.problem: Aim practice in Azimuth is effective but feels like work, and warming up is a chore. A rhythm drill gives the hands a steady, repeatable pace to settle into, set to music you chose, so warming up is something you want to start.
data.audience: Azimuth players: Overwatch players from beginner to intermediate, on desktop with a mouse (mostly Chromium), who want to warm up to their own music.
data.whyNow: v3 added a positional audio engine and a mature drill, level and coach framework, so a music-driven drill can reuse most of what exists.
data.successLooksLike: You'd pick it to warm up. Add a song, pick a difficulty, targets land on the beat, and after a song or two your hand feels loose and accurate. It stands alone in Training and doesn't change the daily warm-up.

elements.title: Constraints

items.text: TypeScript (strict; build runs tsc --noEmit) + Vite 8 + three.js 0.186. No UI framework: screens are template-string HTML in src/ui.
Every drill extends Drill (src/drills/drill.ts), returns a DrillReport (0–100 score, stats, analytics) and is registered in DRILL_DEFS (src/drills/registry.ts) with 10 levels and 1/2/3★ thresholds.
All sound goes through the single WebAudio Audio class (src/core/audio.ts), unlocked from a user gesture. Today it only synthesises sounds; it does not play samples or music files yet.
Static site on GitHub Pages: no server and no accounts. Uploaded audio never leaves the browser.
Desktop Chromium is the main target (pointer lock with unadjustedMovement). Firefox must still work.
Saves are small JSON in localStorage via store (src/core/store.ts), with backup export/import in Settings → Your data. Audio files cannot be stored there (~5 MB limit).
Shots resolve at the instant of the click: Game.button() calls fire() and then drill.onShot() synchronously inside the mousedown handler (ShotResult.at is game-clock time).
Tests are vitest in a node environment (tests/*.test.ts). Beat detection, chart building and scoring must be pure functions that run without WebAudio or the DOM.
No copyrighted music in the repo. There is no built-in song; test audio is generated by a test-only helper (D11).
All copy is in plain words for beginners, in the same voice as the coach and Field Manual.

elements.title: How do notes reach you?

data.question: How do notes reach you?
data.outcome: Targets spawn in the 3D range on chosen beats, as a mix of target types that appear at different times. Each type behaves differently but in time with the music (e.g. a player figure that strafes to the beat, shaped flick icons that pop up rhythmically), and disappears if it isn't hit in time. The feel is a mix of Beat Saber and Guitar Hero, but as an aim trainer.

data.question: Which target types are in the first version?
data.outcome: Flick shapes, Peekers, Holds, Decoys, Bursts, Strafers

options.label: Flick shapes
options.summary: Orbs and shaped icons pop up on the beat and must be shot before they fade. The shape tells you what kind of flick it is. Trains short and wide flicks.

options.label: Strafers
options.summary: A player figure spawns on a beat and strafes, changing direction on the beat (ADAD in time with the music). Take it down before the phrase ends or it leaves. Trains tracking.

options.label: Holds
options.summary: An orb glides along a path for a few beats. Hold fire and stay on it. Like Guitar Hero sustains and Beat Saber arcs. Trains smooth tracking.

options.label: Bursts
options.summary: A quick run of small orbs on fast beats (eighth notes) in a line or arc. Tap through them in order. Like Beat Saber chains. Trains quick switching.

options.label: Peekers
options.summary: A head peeks out from behind a wall on the beat and hides again on the next. Be there first. Trains crosshair placement.

options.label: Echo notes
options.summary: A ping from beside or behind you lands on the beat. Turn the short way and hit the target. Trains sound awareness, reusing the Echo drill's 3D audio.

options.label: Decoys
options.summary: A friendly figure is mixed into the pattern. Don't shoot it: hitting it breaks your combo. Trains trigger discipline.

data.rationale: Chosen by the human in "Which target types should be in the first version? Each one trains a different aim skill, and all of them spawn on the beat and vanish if missed."

data.question: How does an uploaded song become a chart?
data.outcome: Fully automatic: the drill detects tempo and beats and places targets on the beat grid, with busier patterns in louder parts. Drop a song in and play. There is no preview or fix-up screen.

options.label: Automatic + quick fix
options.summary: Auto analysis plus a preview screen to tap or nudge tempo and first beat.

options.label: Tap it yourself
options.summary: The player taps the beat to build the chart.

data.rationale: Chosen by the human in the Song → chart comparison: fastest path from upload to playing.
consequences: Beat analysis must be robust on its own: there is no human correction step.

Adding a song may ask for a style preset and difficulty (D7, D9), but never for tempo or beat corrections.

data.question: How should an uploaded song become a chart?

sides.label: Fully automatic

elements.title: Do you have to hit on the beat, or just before the target is gone?

data.question: Do you have to hit on the beat, or just before the target is gone?
data.outcome: Window + beat bonus. A target appears on a beat and stays for a hit window. Any hit inside the window counts, but a hit close to the target's own beat scores Perfect and builds the combo faster. Higher levels shrink the window towards the beat.

options.label: On the beat
options.summary: Exact beat, ±60 ms graded; else a miss.

options.label: Before it's gone
options.summary: Any hit in the window counts; sooner scores more.

options.label: Window + beat bonus
options.summary: Any hit in the window counts; on-beat hits score Perfect.

data.rationale: Chosen by the human: rhythm feel without punishing the stop-then-click habit the coach teaches.
consequences: Judgement words are Perfect (within the Perfect width of the target beat), Early (in the window, before that), Late (in the window, after it) and Miss (window ended).

Timing per target: launchTime = landTime − 1 beat (fly-in); landTime = targetTime − leadBeats; windowEnd = targetTime + afterBeats. leadBeats, afterBeats and the Perfect width come from the level table (T5).
Timing stats (mean signed offset in ms) come from hits, for the debrief and coach.
rejectedOutcomes: Before it's gone with no beat bonus

elements.title: How are charts generated so that any song gets a good chart?

data.question: How are charts generated so that any song gets a good chart?
data.outcome: Each song is analysed for its structure (beats, bars, sections, energy, onsets). When you add a song you choose presets that shape how its chart is built: a style preset (a probabilistic matrix weighting target types and density per section kind) and a difficulty (D9). The generator samples spawns bar by bar from the style matrix, scaled by the level the difficulty resolves to, seeded by song + preset + level so the same inputs always give the same chart. No song needs a hand-made chart. The MVP ships one style preset, Mixed (D8); the others are on the roadmap.
data.rationale: The human's comments on V3 and D7: many songs in the long run, so charts must be generated from each song's own structure via a probabilistic decision matrix, with a few basic presets picked when adding a song to alter how it's structured. Start with one preset for the MVP so it can be tested, and keep the rest on the roadmap.
consequences: Song analysis must find sections, not only beats.
Presets are data: one matrix per preset, plus optional multipliers on the level table's target parameters (e.g. strafer health × 1.5 for a future Tracker preset).
The seed uses the level, not the difficulty, because the level inside a band changes as you unlock (D17).
Adding a song shows a preset picker; with only Mixed in the MVP it defaults to Mixed so adding stays one step.
Roadmap presets: Quick taps, Tracker, Incoming (see scope, later).

elements.title: Notes drift out of sync with the music. The game clock runs on requestAnimationFrame and freezes on pause, while music plays on the AudioContext clock, and output latency (especially Bluetooth headphones) adds 20–250 ms.

data.risk: Notes drift out of sync with the music. The game clock runs on requestAnimationFrame and freezes on pause, while music plays on the AudioContext clock, and output latency (especially Bluetooth headphones) adds 20–250 ms.
data.mitigation: Position every target from song time (AudioContext time minus output latency minus the audio offset), never from accumulated frame time. Pausing stops the music source and freezes song time; it does not suspend the shared AudioContext, so menu sounds keep working. A tap-along calibration and a manual slider set the audio offset.

elements.title: Automatic analysis picks the wrong tempo or beat phase on some songs (live recordings, swing, tempo changes, long quiet intros), so targets feel off-beat and there's no way for the player to fix it.

data.risk: Automatic analysis picks the wrong tempo or beat phase on some songs (live recordings, swing, tempo changes, long quiet intros), so targets feel off-beat and there's no way for the player to fix it.
data.mitigation: Use onset-strength autocorrelation with a tempo prior (prefer 80–180 BPM, resolving half and double tempo) and track beats per section rather than one global grid. Score the analysis confidence; when it's low, place targets on detected onsets (audible hits) instead of a strict grid. Test against generated songs with swing, tempo ramps and noise in vitest.

elements.title: Four cues at once (fly-in, ring, pulse, beat strip) clutter dense charts at high levels, so players can't see the targets they're aiming at.

data.risk: Four cues at once (fly-in, ring, pulse, beat strip) clutter dense charts at high levels, so players can't see the targets they're aiming at.
data.mitigation: Keep each cue thin and low-contrast except at the moment it matters (ring and flash on the beat), cap targets on screen per level, and let the beat strip be switched off in Settings. Playtest level 10 on a fast song before tuning.

elements.title: Section detection mislabels the song (e.g. calls a quiet verse a peak, or finds no peak in a flat electronic loop), so charts feel random or monotonous.

data.risk: Section detection mislabels the song (e.g. calls a quiet verse a peak, or finds no peak in a flat electronic loop), so charts feel random or monotonous.
data.mitigation: Classify sections by smoothed energy tiers and change points rather than trying to name verse or chorus; enforce a minimum section length (4 bars, snapped to bar boundaries); and fall back to energy-only density when the change points are weak. Unit-test on generated songs with known quiet/loud structure.

A group of beats, normally four. The generator works bar by bar.

A kind of target with its own look and behaviour (D2). `kind` on ChartTarget.
The beat a target should be hit on. `targetTime` in code (seconds of song time).
From landTime (the target lands) to windowEnd. Any hit inside counts; when it ends without a hit the target is missed and removed.
How a hit is graded: Perfect (within the Perfect width of the target beat), Early or Late (elsewhere in the window), or Miss.
Seconds into the song as the player hears it: AudioContext time since the music started, minus output latency, minus the audio offset. Everything in a run is timed from it.
The four ways the beat is shown (D5): fly-in, closing ring, pulse and the beat strip.
The Guitar Hero-style HUD strip at the bottom of the screen where icons of upcoming targets scroll to a hit line.
How late the player hears the audio, in ms. It is subtracted in song time, so a positive offset makes targets arrive later. Set by the tap-along calibration or by hand.

elements.title: Drop in a song and be playing it within seconds, with no setup.

data.statement: Drop in a song and be playing it within seconds, with no setup.
data.why: Bringing your own music is the hook. Any friction before the first target kills it as a warm-up.
checks: Uploading an MP3, WAV or OGG file (plus M4A/AAC on Chromium) starts analysis immediately; an unsupported or broken file shows a plain-words error instead of failing silently.
A 4-minute song is analysed in under 5 s on a mid-range laptop, and the page never freezes for more than 100 ms while it runs.
Uploaded songs are stored in the browser (IndexedDB) and are still in the song list after a reload, with no re-upload.
The preset picker shown when adding a song has sensible defaults, so upload → playing takes at most one extra click.
The same song, preset and level always produce the same chart (seeded generator), so scores are comparable between runs.
Any song gets a chart with no hand-authoring: generation uses only the song's analysis, the preset and the level (D7).

elements.title: Targets land on the beat of the music.

data.statement: Targets land on the beat of the music.
data.why: If timing feels off, it's not a rhythm drill, and an automatic chart has no fix-up step (D3).
checks: On generated test songs (drum loops at 70–190 BPM, with swing, noise and a quiet intro), detected tempo is within 1% and beat times within 20 ms of the truth (vitest, node).
During play, every target's spawn and hit time is computed from the AudioContext clock; drift between chart and audio stays under 10 ms across a 4-minute song.
Pausing stops music and targets together, and resuming continues in sync.
An audio offset (from a short tap-along calibration or set by hand) shifts every target; after calibration, the player's taps average within ±20 ms of the beat.

elements.title: Six target types each spawn on the beat, behave in time with the music and vanish if missed.

data.statement: Six target types each spawn on the beat, behave in time with the music and vanish if missed.
data.why: A mix of target types is the core idea (D1, D2): each one trains a different aim skill inside one musical run.
checks: Flick shapes, strafers, holds, bursts, peekers and decoys all appear in charts.
Every target spawns on a beat (or eighth beat for bursts) and is removed when its hit window ends without a hit.
Strafers change direction on beats; holds move along their path in step with the beat; peekers show and hide on beats.
Hitting a decoy counts as a mistake and breaks the combo.

elements.title: It is a first-class Azimuth drill: levels, stars, debrief, Logbook and coaching.

data.statement: It is a first-class Azimuth drill: levels, stars, debrief, Logbook and coaching.
data.why: Players already understand Azimuth's progression. A rhythm drill outside it would feel like a toy.
checks: Registered in DRILL_DEFS with 10 levels and 1/2/3★ thresholds, and listed in Training like the other drills; not added to DAILY and the streak is unchanged (D15).
Picking a difficulty plays the highest unlocked level inside its band; a star on a level unlocks the next level in that band (D10, D17).
Its DrillReport gives a 0–100 score, the difficulty and level played, timing stats (mean early/late offset in ms) and hit rate per target type.
Flick-type hits produce FlickRecords, so the existing coach findings and film room work on them.
Runs appear in the Logbook's recent sessions.

elements.title: It feels like a rhythm game, not a test: flowing, musical and satisfying.

data.statement: It feels like a rhythm game, not a test: flowing, musical and satisfying.
data.why: The brief: a warm-up you want to start. Beat Saber and Guitar Hero are the references.
checks: Every hit gives instant feedback (sound, flash and a judgement word: Perfect, Early or Late) within one frame of the click; a missed target shows Miss as it vanishes.
A hit within the Perfect width of the target's beat scores more and adds more to the combo than a hit elsewhere in the window (D4).
A combo counter and multiplier build on consecutive hits and visibly break on a miss or a decoy hit.
The synthwave scene reacts to the music: the grid scrolls at the tempo and glows on the beat (D6).
Playtest: the human plays it on their own songs and says it feels on-beat and fun enough to warm up with.

elements.title: Define Overdrive's song, analysis and chart types

data.title: Define Overdrive's song, analysis and chart types
data.description: src/rhythm/types.ts holds types only, plus `as const` lists DIFFICULTIES, SECTION_KINDS, TARGET_KINDS and FLICK_SHAPES. SongMeta {id: SHA-256 hex of the file bytes, name: file name without extension, mime, duration: seconds, addedAt: ISO string, preset: PresetId, difficulty}. Analysis (T3) {version, sampleRate, duration, bpm, beats: number[] seconds, beatEnergy: number[], onsetEnv: Float32Array, onsetHop: seconds per envelope frame, confidence: 0..1}. It has no downbeats. Structure (T4) {downbeats: number[], bars: number[] bar start times, sections: Section[]} with Section {startBar, endBar (exclusive), kind}. PresetRow {weights: Record<TargetKind, number>, perBar: {from, to}}, Preset {id, name, rows: Record<SectionKind, PresetRow>, flickShapes: Record<FlickShape, number>, params?: multipliers}. ChartTarget is a union on kind; every target has launchTime, landTime, targetTime, windowEnd (seconds of song time) and position {bearing, pitch, distance}. Bearing is in degrees clockwise, matching dirFrom() in src/drills/common.ts; pitch is in degrees up; distance is in metres. For figures (strafer, peeker, decoy), position is the ground point and pitch is ignored. FlickTarget adds shape; BurstTarget adds orbs: {time, position}[] and counts as one target in density; Strafer, Hold and Peeker add their params. Wall {bearing, distance, width, height}. Chart {songId, preset, difficulty, level, duration, targets, walls}.
doneWhen: src/rhythm/types.ts exports everything above and `npm run typecheck` passes.
Comments on each type cite the glossary term it implements (Song, Chart, Style preset, Target, Target beat, Hit window).

elements.title: Detect tempo, beats and onsets from PCM

data.title: Detect tempo, beats and onsets from PCM
data.description: src/rhythm/analysis.ts: analyse(pcm: mono Float32Array, sampleRate) → Analysis (T1; no downbeats, which belong to T4). Spectral-flux onset envelope (~10 ms hop) using a small radix-2 FFT written in src/rhythm/fft.ts, with no new npm packages. Tempo by autocorrelation with a prior preferring 80–180 BPM and resolving half/double tempo; dynamic-programming beat tracking so local drift is followed; per-beat RMS energy; a 0..1 confidence. Export ANALYSIS_VERSION = 1 and stamp it on every Analysis. No DOM or WebAudio.
doneWhen: vitest: on songgen loops at 70–190 BPM, including swing, noise and an 8 s quiet intro, tempo is within 1% and at least 95% of beats fall within 20 ms of the truth.

Beatless noise returns confidence below 0.4; every songgen loop returns at least 0.6.
package.json dependencies are unchanged.

elements.title: Split songs into bars and sections by energy

data.title: Split songs into bars and sections by energy
data.description: src/rhythm/sections.ts: structure(analysis) → Structure (T1). Estimate downbeats from the accent pattern across the four beat phases, build bars, smooth bar energy and find change points. The first section is always intro and the last always outro; middle sections are classified by energy tier as calm, build (rising) or peak. Sections are at least 4 bars, bar-aligned, with endBar exclusive. Fall back to energy-only tiers when change points are weak (R4). The worker (T9) caches Analysis and Structure together.

elements.title: Generate seeded charts from analysis, preset and level

data.title: Generate seeded charts from analysis, preset and level
data.description: src/rhythm/generator.ts: generate(analysis, structure, preset, level, songId) → Chart. PRNG (e.g. mulberry32) seeded by hash(songId, preset id, level). For each bar: take the section row, draw a count from perBar (ramped across build sections) × level density, choose slots weighted by onset strength (on beats; burst orbs on eighths), and sample each type from the row weights and each flick's shape from the shape split. Times: targetTime = the slot; landTime = targetTime − leadBeats; launchTime = landTime − 1 beat; windowEnd = targetTime + afterBeats. Positions: on-screen spread within ±35° bearing and −10..+15° pitch at 10–18 m for most types; triangles 60–150° left or right; peekers get a Wall in chart.walls. Cap concurrent targets at maxConcurrent, and never overlap strafers or holds with each other. When analysis.confidence < 0.4 (R2), slots come from detected onset peaks instead of the beat grid. The chart ends at the song's end (D12).
doneWhen: The same inputs give a deep-equal chart; a different songId gives a different one.
Over a 200-bar synthetic song, type frequencies per section kind are within ±5% of the preset matrix.
For confident analyses every targetTime lies on a beat (an eighth for burst orbs) within 1 ms; for low-confidence analyses every targetTime lies on an onset peak.
Concurrent targets never exceed maxConcurrent, and no two strafer/hold targets overlap in time.

elements.title: Judge hits, track the combo and compute the 0–100 score

data.title: Judge hits, track the combo and compute the 0–100 score
data.description: src/rhythm/scoring.ts: judge(songTimeOfClick, target, level) → perfect | early | late | miss, plus a signed offset in ms (D4 consequences). Combo and multiplier ×1→×4, stepping up every 8 combo points; Perfect adds 2, Early or Late adds 1, Miss resets. Decoys: a hit resets the combo and costs points; leaving one alone is neutral; decoys are left out of hit rate and vanish with no Miss. Burst hit rate counts each orb. Strafers and holds score the fraction of their life spent on target while firing; under 30% counts as a miss for the combo. Final 0–100 score plus stats: mean signed offset, hit rate per target type and max combo.
doneWhen: Unit tests cover perfect, early, late and miss at the window and Perfect boundaries.

A decoy hit resets the combo; an ignored decoy changes nothing (test).

data.title: Create the Overdrive drill core
data.description: src/drills/overdrive.ts: OverdriveDrill extends Drill (id 'overdrive', movable = false, D13). Launch path: DrillDef.make gains an optional third argument, make(g, level, ctx?), and startDrill forwards it; Overdrive's make requires ctx = {chart, buffer}. duration = chart.duration + 2, and done is set once songTime() passes chart.duration (Game ends runs on the frame clock). begin() starts the music. update() reads audio.songTime() to launch targets, advance them through fly-in → landed → window → expired, and remove expired ones as misses. doneWhen: The human plays it on their own songs and says it feels on-beat and fun (G5).
No target is unreadable at Expert on a fast song.
The tuned values are committed in presets.ts and levels.ts, and `npm test` is green.
